abstract: How disease spreads across space is well studied, but how the topology of spatial networks shapes host-parasite evolution is less understood. Host-parasite interactions unfold across spatial networks in which populations differ in the number of neighbours, yet most theory has focused on regular networks such as grids. Here, we embed a multilocus gene-for-gene infection model into a metapopulation to investigate host-parasite coevolution across empirically inspired and synthetic spatial networks. We find that variation in the number of neighbours generates spatial variation in local host density and parasite prevalence, creating a network-wide mosaic of ecological conditions for selection. Greater variation in the number of neighbours, or higher degree heterogeneity, promotes the evolution of host resistance. The same degree heterogeneity leads to reduced parasite infectivity in well-connected patches versus higher infectivity in patches with fewer neighbours. Both outcomes arise because populations with fewer neighbours experience net host outflux and reduced prevalence, whereas populations with more neighbours accumulate hosts and experience different selective pressures. Dispersal both drives and homogenises host resistance across the network, while maintaining spatial structure in parasite infectivity. We here identify a topology-epidemiology-evolution feedback impacting coevolution even when populations experience identical environmental conditions. Across network types, coevolutionary outcomes are driven by the network's degree heterogeneity, which can be quantified using the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index in real landscapes. Our results provide testable predictions for how changes in network topology can shape the evolution of host resistance and parasite infectivity.
